target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection is ethically justified because most specimens are already dead and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts
objection: The “already dead” framing is not a safe basis for permission because dissection programs typically rely on harmful supply chains; AG2 says roughly 99% of dissection animals are caught in the wild, and that wild-catching reduces local populations and biodiversity.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection supply typically depends on wild capture and biodiversity-harming sourcing
objection: That sourcing picture is said not to match many school dissections: AG1 argues that over 98% of dissected animals are already deceased and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts destined for landfills, so the wild-capture/biodiversity-harm premise does not describe the typical classroom context.

target: AG1’s claim that real-animal dissection provides unique educational and skill benefits
objection: AG2 objects that synthetic models and computer simulations can teach the same anatomical concepts and can also build lab-relevant skills, so real-animal dissection is not uniquely educational or necessary.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives can teach the same things and make real dissection unnecessary
objection: AG1 argues that models and simulations cannot fully substitute for handling real tissue: real dissection uniquely develops three-dimensional anatomical understanding, tactile problem-solving, fine motor control, and hand-eye coordination under authentic biological variability.

target: AG1’s claim that the “already dead” framing makes dissection ethically acceptable
objection: AG2 says that being already dead does not remove the harms of obtaining specimens, because dissection supply chains often involve wild capture and other damaging practices that reduce local populations and biodiversity.

target: AG2’s claim that models and simulations can teach the same anatomical relationships and skills
objection: AG1 says that assumption is unsupported because real dissection uniquely provides tactile, hands-on experience with actual tissues, anatomical variability, and tool-use practice that alternatives do not match as directly.

target: AG1’s claim that alternatives can match the learning and career benefits of dissection
objection: AG2 says non-animal alternatives can also produce the same learning outcomes and even the same “aha” and career-inspiration effects, so those benefits do not require real-animal dissection.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection generally depends on wild-caught animals and therefore causes ethical/environmental harm
objection: AG1 disputes that this is the typical classroom supply reality, arguing that most specimens are already dead and many fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts, so the wild-capture and biodiversity-harm premise does not govern ordinary school dissection programs.

target: AG1’s claim that real dissection is educationally worthwhile because it gives direct hands-on experience
objection: AG2 says real dissection is still unnecessary because non-animal alternatives can deliver the same curriculum outcomes, and the “already dead” framing does not erase the sourcing harms that remain part of the practice.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is unnecessary because standards and medical training do not require it
objection: AG1 argues that education is not limited to activities literally mandated by standards; schools may legitimately include dissection because it develops deeper anatomical understanding, critical thinking, and psychomotor lab skills, and because the specimens are usually already dead/byproducts.

target: AG1’s claim that alternatives do not match dissection as directly for deep understanding, critical thinking, and motor skills
objection: AG2 says that assumption is weak because high-fidelity models and simulations can teach anatomical relationships, support interpretation and verification, and train motor skills without using dead animals.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is not needed because alternatives cover the same learning goals
objection: AG1 says the target overlooks embodied, tactile learning from real tissue—how structures feel, separate, and vary—which real dissection uniquely teaches and which models or screens cannot replicate with the same fidelity.

target: AG1’s claim that already-dead/byproduct sourcing makes the ethical objection inapplicable
objection: AG2 says that if roughly 99% of dissection animals are wild-caught, then the practice still depends on biodiversity-harming sourcing, so the “already dead” framing does not remove the ethical problem.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is unnecessary and therefore not justified even if educationally useful
objection: AG1 says students can still need real dissection as part of achieving biology course outcomes because different students learn in different ways and dissection provides hands-on competencies and science motivation that alternatives may not supply equally well.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection should be allowed because it is not required by AP Biology, NGSS, or medical training
objection: AG2 argues that if an activity is harmful and not necessary for legitimate educational or medical goals, then it is unjustified; optional enrichment does not outweigh animal and environmental harms.

target: AG2’s claim that because dissection is not required, it is not necessary for core learning outcomes
objection: AG1 says dissection is necessary for embodied lab competencies and authentic anatomical interpretation, so the “not required” standard is too narrow and misses the practical biology skills that real dissection uniquely develops.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is worthwhile enough to justify itself despite not being required
objection: AG2 says “educationally worthwhile” is not enough when the activity is not necessary for the outcomes; without a necessity or unique-benefit link, the harms are not outweighed.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is merely optional enrichment rather than necessary for core biology outcomes
objection: AG1 says that is false because dissection trains embodied lab competencies and real anatomical interpretation under realistic conditions, which models and simulations cannot provide with the same fidelity.

target: AG1’s claim that supervision and opt-outs make the practice ethically acceptable
objection: AG2 says safeguards do not remove upstream harms: even if some specimens are already dead or some students opt out, the school still creates demand for dissection specimens and does not eliminate the sourcing-related animal welfare and biodiversity impacts.

target: AG2’s claim that wild-capture harms remain the relevant ethical problem even for supervised dissection
objection: AG1 says that premise does not generally apply to school dissections because most specimens are already dead and many fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts, so the harms from wild capture are not an unavoidable feature of allowing student dissection.

target: AG1’s claim that schools can usually procure only already-dead/byproduct specimens
objection: AG2 says schools cannot reliably verify and control the full origin of every specimen because vendors and supply chains can substitute sources, so procurement promises cannot ensure that animals were not taken from the wild.

target: AG2’s claim that schools cannot generally manage specimen sourcing to avoid wild-caught animals
objection: AG1 argues schools can often direct purchasing toward established byproduct streams, such as fetal pigs from the meat industry, and require provenance documentation so demand is steered to already-dead/byproduct specimens.

target: AG1’s claim that schools can generally manage sourcing so dissection specimens are already dead or byproducts
objection: AG2 says that is not realistic in practice because schools need large numbers consistently and vendors can fill shortages with wild-caught sources, so byproduct-only contract language does not eliminate upstream harms.

target: AG2’s claim that demand for specimens will force vendors to rely on wild capture when byproduct supply is imperfect
objection: AG1 says byproduct supply can be stable and scalable, especially for common specimens like fetal pigs, and that procurement contracts with provenance requirements can operationalize byproduct-only sourcing rather than forcing wild capture.

target: AG1’s claim that schools can generally procure only already-dead/byproduct animals through contracts and provenance checks
objection: AG2 says schools usually cannot reliably verify or audit upstream origin at the level needed to prevent substitutions or mislabeling, so wild-capture harms remain a realistic part of the supply chain.

target: AG2’s claim that schools cannot generally enforce byproduct-only sourcing
objection: AG1 says schools can specify specimen type, require provenance/lot documentation, and refuse noncompliant shipments, which can direct demand to already-dead/byproduct supply streams and undermine the claim that wild-capture is unavoidable.

target: AG1’s claim that provenance documents and contract terms can guarantee byproduct-only sourcing
objection: AG2 says lot-level paperwork is often just vendor declaration, schools lack auditing power over the full supply chain, and substitutions or upstream wild-capture can still occur, so schools cannot generally guarantee the sourcing standard AG1 relies on.
